result.summary: Pausanias describes the Pamisus river and its fish, then the coastal towns of Messenia: Corone, with its temples and the tale of its name, Colonides, and Asine, whose people are descended from the Dryopes. He ends with the nearby promontory, island and harbour.

scenes.title: The Pamisus and river beasts
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Pamisus, its clear water and sea fish, and compares Greek rivers with the dangerous rivers of other lands.

scenes.title: Corone and its temples
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Corone, its sites, the origin of its name, its statues and the ancient temple of Apollo Corydus.

scenes.title: Colonides
scenes.summary: The people of Colonides claim Attic origin under Colaenus and later took on Dorian ways.

scenes.title: Asine and the Dryopes
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives two accounts of how the Dryopes, defeated by Hercules, came to Asine, and describes the nearby coast.
scenes.stakes: The Dryopes risk captivity and loss of their homeland after defeat by Hercules.

alias_notes.explanation: Ino was worshipped under the name Leucothea.
Title under which Apollo is called at his temple near Corone.

analysis.text: Pausanias links places to etymologies, founding legends and cult, showing how local identity rests on tradition.
The Dryopes' rival accounts and the Messenian restoration by the Thebans show how migration and politics shaped local memory.

language_notes.text: A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 180–200 metres, so 80 stades is about 15 kilometres.
Mullets are sea fish that also enter rivers and feed along muddy bottoms.
Glanides are a kind of fish, probably catfish (silurus). Pausanias compares them with the man-eating river beasts of foreign rivers.
'Sea dogs' are marine animals, probably sharks, that come up the river. Pausanias denies they are true river creatures.
Ino, daughter of Cadmus, leapt into the sea and became the sea goddess Leucothea ('White Goddess').
The Thebans under Epaminondas restored the Messenians to their land after 370 BC. Epimelides is named here as the founder of the town.
Corone sounds like the Greek word for crow (korone), so the crow finding explains the name.
Corydus is a cult title of Apollo; its meaning is uncertain, perhaps 'lark' or 'helmeted'.
The Argonauts were the heroes who sailed with Jason in the Argo to fetch the Golden Fleece.
Colænus was led by an oracle to settle where a crested lark (korydallos) led him; the story explains the town's name and its supposed Attic origin.
"In the third generation afterwards" means three generations after the Dryopes were named for their founder, a rough way of dating the event.
Eurystheus was the king of Argos who set Hercules his labours, so his hostility to Hercules explains why he welcomed the Dryopes.
"Plume themselves" means take pride in, like a bird preening its feathers.
A stade was a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet or about 180 metres, so 40 stades is about four and a half miles.

context_notes.text: Pausanias lists famous rivers of distant lands as known for crocodiles and other dangerous animals.
Æsculapius was the god of healing, and Dionysus the god of wine.
Athene was the goddess of wisdom and war, and the crow was one of her sacred birds.
Corone and Colonides lie on the Messenian coast in the south-western Peloponnese, on the Messenian Gulf.
The Messenians were driven out by the Spartans (Lacedæmonians) and later restored to their land, which is the "restoration" meant here.
Delphi lay in Phocis, yet its people disliked being called Phocians, which shows that regional names could carry prestige or shame.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias sets the gentle Greek rivers against the dangerous foreign ones, flattering Greece's own waters.
An origin tale explains the town's name through the crow, a story of the kind Pausanias often reports.
Pausanias openly admits ignorance, which shows his honest, careful stance as a traveller-historian.
Pausanias sets the Asinæi against the Eubœans of Styra, who disown the same ancestry, to highlight differing attitudes to the same origin.
The Asinæi are shown as proud of their ancestry, with their temples imitating those of their old home, which marks them out as a people clinging to their past.
